subtopic: POSSIBLE TRANSFER OF JURISDICTION TO PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my absence yesterday, while I was detained in Quebec by illness, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked the right hon. Prime Minister various questions concerning Indians in Canada.
I must, first of all, give the hon. members the assurance that there is no question of transferring the jurisdiction over the Indian people from the federal to the provincial governments. We intend, as a government, to maintain all the rights granted to them under the constitution on Indian affairs in this country. On the other hand, everybody recognizes that the Indians, being citizens living in various provinces, should benefit like any other citizen from certain provincial services. We feel that the extension of those services to the Indian people in the various provinces does not prevent in any way the federal government from maintaining its jurisdiction.
That is why, following the federal-provincial conference held in December 1963, it was decided, in co-operation with the various provinces, to call a federal-provincial conference which would deal only with Indian affairs in order to bring about a change in methods and to apply other and more appropriate methods so that the Indians might benefit from those provincial services; that conference was scheduled for the end of May. In view of the scope of the matter to be discussed, it was decided to postpone the conference until the end of October; it will therefore take place October 29 and 30 next in Ottawa.
As it so happens we shall be discussing measures that would enable the provinces to extend a number of provincial services to the Indians, on condition the federal government grant compensation. The very important problem of consultation on Indian affairs has been raised. I can assure the two hon. members and the entire house, that the present government will not make any major decision during this parliament before consulting the Indians themselves, as they are the first concerned in all these measures and, all the more so, provincial authorities.
I therefore think these various answers are such that both hon. members will be satisfied.

Mr. Chairman, I want to repeat here that if the estimates of my department are placed before the house today, it is because of my promise to allow hon. members to state their views on the way the Canadian constitution might be amended from now on, no longer by the United Kingdom parliament in London, but rather by the Canadian parliament itself, in other words, on the way to repatriate our constitution.
It has been agreed between the various parties, through all the house leaders, that there will be no general discussion today on item 1 of the estimates. The house will have the opportunity to discuss that in a fortnight.
How will it be possible to turn the document known so far as the British North America Act into a really Canadian document, by providing that the structures it sanctions might be amended exclusively in Canada? That is certainly the main legal question we are interested in as legislators.
The history of this undertaking includes already many episodes which have taken place during a long period. May I recall them briefly.
The first federal-provincial conference which discussed constitutional amendments was held in 1927. The then minister of justice, one of the great Canadians we have known, Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, championed the cause and held the firm belief that the Canadian authorities should have the power to amend the British North America Act. At that time however, the opinions were much divided as to whether it was appropriate that this power should be given to us.
In 1935, a special committee of this house considered the problem but could not reach a definite conclusion. The matter was placed

before a provincial conference during that same year, and in 1936, recommendations were prepared by officials. Once more, there was no agreement and it was impossible to act in a positive manner.
It was necessary to wait until after the war to resume the discussions. Following the amendments to the federative act in 1949, a constitutional conference with the premiers was called. A subcommittee of the attorneys general was set up. During two meetings they analysed all the aspects of the problem, but, once more, without reaching an agreement.
The attorneys general resumed the task in 1960 and 1961, in the course of four meetings. From these long consultations between the federal government and the various provincial governments emerged an amendment formula expressed in a bill. This bill was entitled: "An act for the amendment in Canada of the Canadian constitution". The bill was published in order that its principles might be discussed in all possible circles. However, last summer, after nearly three years, certain provinces were still reluctant about expressing a definite opinion concerning that formula, and others had expressed reservations.
Yet, one could see that everyone was truly desirous of reaching an agreement on an acceptable solution. That is why the prime ministers and premiers felt that they should go over the question once more during the federal-provincial conference held in Charlottetown early this month. The best way to report the results of the ensuing discussions is to read into the record the press release they issued following the Charlottetown conference.
I shall read from the official version in French but I have sent the official English version to the interpreters so that the text which will be read in either language will be exactly the same as the one which was approved by the prime ministers and premiers in Charlottetown.
The prime ministers and premiers affirmed their unanimous decision to conclude the repatriation of the BJST.A. Act without delay. To this end, they decided to complete a procedure for amending the constitution in Canada, based on the draft legislation proposed at the constitutional conference of 1961, which they accept in principle. An early meeting of the attorneys general of Canada and the provinces will be held to complete the amending formula devised by the 1961 conference, and to report to the prime ministers and premiers.

The attorneys general have thus been given terms of reference for a meeting which is to

take place in Ottawa on Monday and Tuesday next, and from which we hope to report to the premiers who will be meeting in the following week.
I do not think it would be appropriate for me at this time, in advance of the conference, to express my views as to how this long process of discussion and negotiation can be brought to a satisfactory conclusion. I am most anxious to hear the views and recommendations of members in all parts of the house. This is a matter on which we are all agreed as to the objective. As long as we cannot amend our own constitution there is a very real sense in which we lack an essential pillar in the structure of our confederation. There is, we all recognize, a deformity to be remedied.
It is equally clear from the history of the matter that the remedy involves genuine difficulties. Any satisfactory constitution requires in its amending formula a careful balance between the virtue of security, of constitutional safeguards, and the necessity of some flexibility in order to adapt to changing requirements. A federal constitution, of course, must achieve this balance within the framework of federal-provincial jurisdictions which are fundamental to the structure of the constitution.
Our predecessors have struggled with this problem for many years. I believe they have gradually moved us to a position in which we can look forward now to an agreed solution which will make our constitution Canadian. I know that is the wish of everyone in this house, and I can assure the house that the government will listen attentively to all the advice offered to it for this purpose, which stands far above any partisanship.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has said that our predecessors had struggled over this question, and I would admit quite quickly to this committee that I am joining in the struggle. However, the minister avoided a favourite term of one of his colleagues, the minister of defence. He did not use the words "new hard facts", which is one of the favourite cliches of the Minister of National Defence. So because we have no new hard facts to add to a most interesting constitutional development historically it makes an intelligent exchange difficult.
In the Rowell-Sirois recommendations there is what might be called a statement of purpose, and I think this would be a good place to commence my remarks:
In the course of our work we have come to appreciate as never before the achievements of the
[Mr. Favreau.l
fathers of confederation.. .By their achievements they laid the foundation of national unity and of the federal system, both of which our instructions enjoin us to respect. It is our hope, and we venture to say our confident expectation, that they accomplished these great things without laying on future generations the dead hand of the past and that they transmitted to us a constitution capable of development not only through judicial interpretation but through amendment as well, to meet the new situations and problems which were bound to arise... Canadians are so proudly conscious of the national unity which they have achieved and so respectful of the federal system that has made this unity possible that there may be some danger of their thinking of national unity and of the federal system in the abstract as having some special merits which make them desirable in themselves. We have endeavoured to keep before us at all times the goal of human welfare which should determine the character of both political and economic systems.
It is interesting to go back to statements which have been made, even though it was just over a generation ago, and try to recall the mood of the country at the time.
I am grateful for a chance to participate in this discussion, and I am also conscious, as anyone who has taken a look at the frustration, shall I say, or at the problems which have faced others through the years must be, that we today are joining in quite a company of greats. I am not going to catalogue them; the minister has mentioned one or two, and they include some of the great parliamentarians of Canada as well as some learned in the academics.
I feel that as a preliminary comment I might put this oft times obscure subject into perspective, or at least into my perspective. First of all, the British North America Act is a Canadian document. It was conceived in Canada and received a great deal of its impetus from conferences which we had 100 years ago in Charlottetown and in Quebec; and we, of course, are taking part in these celebrations. The B.N.A. Act was not imposed on a long suffering colony by an imperial master.
We are busy celebrating the anniversary now, and as the minister says, we are still debating how to detach the act from the statute books of the United Kingdom. I think the minister and most hon. members would agree that we should not be lured by simple or overly simple shibboleths, that all will be well in Canada if only the constitution is returned home. I have read this oversimplification.
The plain fact is that in 1867 when the act passed through its various stages in the United Kingdom parliament hardly a word was changed in the draft act submitted by Canada. At no time in the intervening years

has that parliament objected to the policy involved or the subject matter of any amendment we have sought. Rather, plaintive cries have come out from the United Kingdom house suggesting to us that it is high time we performed our own amending functions. As a matter of fact, in reading the accounts of the passage of the British North America Act through parliament I came across a suggestion that several of the members were asleep. This fact, of course, would have no relevancy today. I also read that the subject succeeding the British North America Act in the United Kingdom house was on the taxing of dogs in the city of London.
I think it is safe to say that no one in this parliament, as the minister has said, objects to the plan to bring the constitution home. I hope it is safe to say that no one seriously thinks that merely by transferring the statute from one jurisdiction to another all our problems will be solved and we will usher in the promised land.
In passing it is interesting to recall that the move to call Canada the kingdom of Canada came particularly from the Quebec delegation. What a dangerous lapse into colonialism was avoided by the use of the word "dominion".
I have one or two questions I should like to pose to the minister. The opposition and the house is being asked to put forward views on a matter that really cannot be discussed constructively without a knowledge of the position of the government. The minister said that he wants to hear our views, but he will not give us his.
We have been told that section 91 is being examined. I want to ask, what is the government's stand on this section? Is the government prepared to surrender to the provinces powers allocated under that section to the federal parliament? If the government is not prepared to consider giving up powers, why is the section being examined? If the government is prepared to surrender certain powers, what powers does this include? I should like to know the government's position relative to section 91. I suggest that these are legitimate questions, without the answer to which parliament is placed in a very awkward position. I am aware of the communique from Charlottetown, but I am wondering what agreements were reached in Charlottetown in this connection.
Was it a condition of repatriation that section 91 should be looked into with a view to transferring certain powers from the

government of Canada to the provinces, and did the government of Canada agree to them? Is the government preparing to concede certain jurisdictional prerogatives, or to accept prior recommendations from the provinces on matters affecting immigration, tariffs and monetary policy, as indicated in certain press reports? In short, Mr. Chairman, I want to know what is the government's policy. Is the government accepting the so-called Fulton formula in its entirety? How is it that what was not acceptable when the formula was first advanced, is now accepted, and what if any are the conditions of such acceptance?
The main problem we face, of course, as the minister said, is to find a formula for amending the constitution when it finally finds domicile here in Canada. I should like to recall that of the dozen or so substantial amendments since 1867, nearly all have come about because of the growth of the country and did not involve any infringement, in the narrow sense of that term, on provincial rights.
Sometimes a loose formula was used for consulting the provinces before seeking amendment. In law I suggest there is nothing to prevent this parliament from seeking and obtaining "any amendment whatsoever in the B.N.A. Act", to quote a statement made by Premier Jean Lesage in 1949. The accuracy of that statement was conceded by the then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, about that time. So this parliament could in law secure an amendment, or even repeal its sections guaranteeing the use of the French language, or provincial control of the schools. I am quick to admit that this is mere legal theory -in fact no government of Canada, I am glad to say, would dare abridge fundamental provincial rights in this regard. Most members would agree that this parliament should not possess the unilateral amending power it now has, but as a matter of political prudence it would not dare exercise.
The first task facing the meeting of the attorneys general is to agree on a definite and reasonable rule about consultations before seeking amendments that will become in every sense the Canadian constitution. As E. A. Driedger, the deputy minister of justice, said in the Canadian Bar Journal, volume 5, 1962:
Our constitution, as in the case of the United Kingdom, consists in part of written material and in part of conventions and customs. The written material consists-partly of our own statutes and. partly of United Kingdom statutes.

He then states:
The present situation may be represented by a circle divided into three segments. One segment represents the authority of the parliament of Canada to make constitutional laws. Another segment represents similar authority possessed by the legislatures of the provinces. The remaining segment represents the area of jurisdiction that is beyond the authority of parliament or the legislature; the sole power to make constitutional laws in this area rests with the parliament of the United Kingdom.
This is what we are trying to bring to an end. Then Mr. Driedger says:
In addition, the parliament of the United Kingdom has concurrent jurisdiction over the federal and provincial segments.
The problem of finding a suitable method of amending the constitution of Canada in Canada involves two things. First there must be transferred to appropriate legislative bodies in Canada jurisdiction over that segment of our circle that is now within the exclusive authority of the parliament of the United Kingdom. Second, we must remove from the parliament of the United Kingdom the jurisdiction it now has over this segment, and also the concurrent jurisdiction it now possesses over the areas included in the segments of our circle now falling within the jurisdiction of parliament or of the legislatures. At the same time, we must be careful to see that we do not now interfere with the powers that parliament and the legislatures have. We would not want, for example, an amending formula that would make it impossible for the provinces alone to amend their constitutions, a power they now possess under head (1) of section 92; nor would we want to take away from parliament the powers it now has under the various sections of the British North America Act that confer upon parliament power to amend the constitution of Canada in matters of purely federal concern. However, it should be pointed out-
This was made clear, I think, during the 1960 conferences.
-that there is some objection to the wide powers conferred on parliament by the new head (1) of section 91 and it is no doubt felt by some that if we do arrive at an acceptable amending formula there should be some change in the authority conferred by this provision.
In any discussion of such a subject it is important, I suggest, to distinguish between rights in a narrow or parochial or provincial sense and the basic rights of a culture or of a group. These latter rights, I suggest, include language, education and religion, to name but three. These are and must continue to be sacrosanct. The success of the early fathers of confederation, and I suggest they were successful, is, it seems to me, largely due to the fact that this difference was acknowledged both in the statute and, equally as important, in the mood and philosophy of the statesmen engaged in the task of making here in this land a viable nation.
If I may philosophize for a moment, I think this is the mood we have to have in Canada
[Mr. Fairweather.l
today, and if we have this mood nothing is impossible for us. Part of this mood was displayed recently in an extraordinary document. It is sometimes frustrating to think that some of the most interesting documents on the constitution and on the state of politics lately have originated not in this chamber but outside this chamber. I am going to recall the appeal for realism in politics published in May of this year in Cite Libre and the Forum. Among many other important things the authors say in considering the subject of federalism:
We believe in federalism as a political structure for Canada. However, we are not satisfied with the evolution of Canadian federalism in a number of areas. As this subject is being discussed ad nauseam nowadays, the mention of one typical area will be quite sufficient.
In those domains which the constitution has given to the jurisdiction of both Ottawa and the provinces, it is evident that plans must be developed jointly. Sharing could also be introduced, if necessary by constitutional amendment, in cases where the establishment of joint plans would permit the population to benefit from important external economies. But one thing is certain: the kind of haphazard political expediency which has inspired so many sharing schemes and federal subsidies for so long has got to stop.
Whatever may be the division of responsibilities between the provinces and the central authority, each must have a share of fiscal powers in proportion to the duties entrusted to it by the constitution.
I want to come for a minute to the so-called Fulton formula and in order to be accurate I shall list some of the main provisions quickly. One of the key provisions in the formula was that all 10 provinces must give their consent before the federal parliament could amend any section of the constitution dealing with basic provincial jurisdiction in the fields of education, language and property and civil rights. Another consideration was that sections dealing only with some provinces and not affecting others could be altered with the consent of the provinces concerned. The third proposal was that general amendments could be made with the approval of two thirds of the provinces provided those seven provinces represent at least half of the Canadian population. Parliament could enact laws in the jurisdiction of the provinces and vice versa provided there was agreement between both levels of government.
This brings to mind a topic that has been of close concern to me for some years. We must find a formula for a sensible delegation of legislation. The example I like to cite is one of very current concern in Canada. I do not think the chairman of the

Toronto stock exchange would go as far as I am going to go but I believe that the 10 provinces should delegate authority over the transfer of stocks and bonds and so on. In other words, this country should be given the opportunity federally to enact the equivalent of the securities and exchange commission of the United States. This is the type of thing I think we have to be prepared to do if we want the discussions with the attorneys general when they are held really to result in something that will make the country work better.
In he Devoir of recent date the great editor of that paper had something to say too about philosophy, and I think that in any consideration of constitutional matters it is worth while recalling his words to the house and putting them on the record. He said:
There is... room for explicit recognition of the special position Quebec-in so far as it is the primary outlet for the French element in Canada- should occupy in the Canadian political organization. But the viewpoint here remains Canadian. One accepts Canada not as a makeshift thing from which one must free oneself, but rather as a political reality that has real value and that one wants to improve. This way of seeing is not unitary but federalist in nature. For it, the federal system is the one that best fits our geographic, historical, economic and political circumstances. Without wanting to preserve this system at all costs, the man thinking this way repudiates the defeatist and sweeping interpretations proposed by certain people to cover the history of the last century.
This way of seeing things also takes into consideration the development that has taken place in Anglo-Canadian opinion during the last quarter century. Those who take this viewpoint believe it is possible and desirable to reform our federal system so that it will be efficient and acceptable for Canadians of both languages. They see this reform as the result of faithful conversations and agreements between the two groups. They'd like to achieve their objectives by way of objective dialogue rather than by means of the ultimatum. But they recognize, to begin with, that it is the Canadian order of things for which they are seeking a solution.
It would be presumptuous for me to say that I share this view. It is the view of one of the great moderates speaking in Canada today. But I accept wholeheartedly the premise and I think it should be said in this discussion involving the very heart of our country.
There is another suggestion I want to make, that when the attorneys general are meeting they consider a formula whereby the bill of rights of Canada, a very important document as it now stands, could become entrenched in the constitution. It should be incorporated into the constitution and it should be so entrenched that no change could be made without the consent of all the legislatures and the parlia-
