ment of Canada. The bill of rights should contain the basic freedoms of religion, speech, press, assembly and association. It should also provide for freedom from discrimination on the grounds of race, colour or creed, freedom from arbitrary arrest and imprisonment and the guarantee of free elections within a stated period. I hope that when this is done, the day will come when concurrent legislation will be enacted in the ten provinces. Then this great formula will be very meaningful, in all the areas of our concern.
Technically and narrowly, Mr. Chairman, and I underline this, the easiest thing for a country would be to have one government or one superstate. However, we are not merely dealing with technicalities and a narrowly conceived formula. We are dealing with a way of life and all that that term implies in social, cultural and in the economic sense. It is for this reason the forthcoming conference which seeks to find this formula and not just bring a piece of paper back across the ocean-that can be done readily-must seek a formula in the same spirit as the men who got together in this country 100 years ago. I hope this does not sound maudlin, as I do not mean it to be. As I said earlier, if that is the type of spirit, and lacking ultimatums, lacking wildly extravagant charges and countercharges, lacking any blackmail or that type of thing, we can make this a viable land.
One of the great contemporary artists who has just completed his latest masterpiece, a new window for the United Nations, once said about his accepted task,
There is so much work to do to get any result. To take a stained glass window and give it life, you have to embrace it, warm it up; you can't deceive God...Well, let's work; let's work.
I think that Mr. Marc Chagall's statement has application in the months ahead. We here, in this type of debate, a non-partisan debate, have a hard and serious responsibility and I suggest that we work, we work.
Mr. B re win: I join with the hon. member for Royal, Mr. Chairman, in welcoming the opportunity afforded by this debate to discuss the vitally important issue of constitutional amendment. I agree with him that this issue, although it seems abstract to some people, vitally affects the human welfare of Canadians and may affect it for generations to come. We here in this party entirely agree with the objective stated by the Minister of Justice, the objective of repatriating the constitution of Canada and making it wholly Canadian. But this statement by itself solves

Supply-Justice
very little. If we adopt the wrong methods in repatriation, and I believe we are in danger of doing so, we may seriously jeopardize the welfare of Canada.
I understand from the statements made by the Prime Minister in this house from time to time, that in the discussions that are to take place next week with the attorneys general of the provinces, the Minister of Justice representing the federal government will, to use the words of the Prime Minister, begin where the last conference left off. I remind the committee that the last conference left off when proposals were made for a formula for amending the Canadian constitution in Canada by the then minister of justice, Hon. Mr. Fulton, on December 1, 1961. This formula became known as the Fulton formula, although of course one should point out the formula was put forward by the administration of that day and supported by them.
This formula was, in fact, incorporated in a draft bill. This bill by section 2 provides, and this is the core of the proposal, that no amendment could be made to the constitution of Canada which affected any provision relating to the powers of the legislatures of the provinces to make laws without the concurrence-mark this-of the legislatures of all the provinces. If it is a fact, Mr. Chairman, that the government of Canada proposes to reintroduce this formula at the forthcoming conference with the attorneys general, then I say to this committee it is necessary to sound a solemn warning, at least a warning as solemn as I can make it.
The carrying out of this proposal has been described by Professor Bora Laskin, an eminent constitutional expert, as an unmitigated constitutional disaster. I adopt his language. Another picturesque phrase has been used to describe this proposal. It has been said, and I think rightly said, it would confine Canada for all time in a constitutional strait-jacket. The burden of my remarks today will be to urge, with all the force I can, that it is the duty of the government of Canada, representing all the people of Canada, to avoid this unmitigated disaster and to avoid unflex-ible provisions for the amending of our constitution.
To many people, Mr. Chairman, constitutions are inclined to be dull, legal documents. But it should never be overlooked that they constitute the framework within which all the activities of government are obliged to operate. They are particularly important in a country such as Canada where we have a federal state and where it is necessary to pre-

serve a reasonable balance between adequate powers for the central government on the one hand, and adequate local autonomy to the provincial governments on the other. It is impossible for the wit of man to devise a distribution of powers and resources available to governments that will stand the test of time. As the first hundred years of Canada's history has clearly revealed, a series of problems have come within the purview of governmental action which were never even contemplated, and indeed could not have been contemplated at the time these constitutional provisions were made.
It is for this reason that an amending procedure in a constitution is absolutely essential, so that a constitution can be adapted to the changing needs of a growing society. We do not have a static society today. This was pointed out by Lord Sankey in a case in the judicial committee where he described the constitution of Canada as a growing tree and not a static document. He sought, by a judicial interpretation, in effect, to amend the British North America Act in the light of that view. But it is impossible to rely on a judicial interpretation as a means of amending the constitution.
A procedure of constitutional amendment which is absolutely rigid and is subject to the veto of small groups of people may condemn Canadian governments in the future to inaction and sterility in the face of serious problems. I remind the committee that in the last 30 years of our history it has been necessary to secure constitutional amendments to permit great social reforms and maintain reasonable standards of social security and a reasonable measure of equality across Canada. The British North America Act, for example, was amended in 1940 to add unemployment insurance to the list of items under section 91 that fall within the competence of this parliament. In 1951 the British North America Act was amended by adding section 94A which permitted the parliament of Canada to make laws in relation to old age pensions, although of course they had made some laws in that regard earlier. This provision confirmed that right. As this house very well knows, we have recently passed a resolution that seeks amendment of the British North America Act to permit the incorporation of survivor benefits in legislation with regard to contributory old age pensions. I should point out to the committee that none of these measures could have been considered or contemplated in 1867 when totally different social conditions prevailed. Yet had the formula which

is put forward, described as the Fulton formula, been in effect and incorporated into law, the result would have been that the legislature of any single province could have prevented effect being given to the general consensus of all the other provinces in Canada in favour of such a constitutional amendment.
Let us take an illustration. I have nothing against the province of Prince Edward Island or its legislature. I understand it is one of the most picturesque and delightful provinces in Canada.
Hear, hear.

Judging by its representatives in this house-and I know there is one applauding at least part of this speech-I believe the people of Prince Edward Island would be reasonable in their views about problems facing the people of Canada as a whole. But the fact of the matter is that in 1961 the total population amounted to 104,000 people, little more than one half of 1 per cent of the population of Canada. The total number of electors in the province is 57,000 out of a total number of Canadian electors of just over 10 million. The electors of the riding of York-Scarborough, in one municipal area of my province, number 162,000 or three times those of Prince Edward Island. The total population of York-Scarborough is 267,000 as compared with the figure of 104,000 which I have already given for Prince Edward Island. I am not trying to single out the province of Prince Edward Island. If I were discussing provinces which might present problems I certainly would not refer to Prince Edward Island. I am merely drawing attention to the complete absurdity of giving a veto over all constitutional amendments to the representatives of a province whose population is numerically less than that of some single constituencies in Canada. I think that even those with the greatest respect for provincial rights-and I myself have great respect for those rights-[DOT] would acknowledge that it would be an absolute absurdity for a single constituency such as York-Scarborough, for example, to be given the power, by its votes, to veto a constitutional amendment for which a consensus of support had been secured across Canada.
I wish to make it clear, however, and in this I follow the remarks of the hon. member for Royal, that there are certain sections of the British North America Act and certain rights which could and should be entrenched in the constitution in such a way that their
Supply-Justice
amendment except by the unanimous consent of the provinces would not be possible. These are matters which are truly fundamental to our whole confederation and with regard to which no change can reasonably be contemplated. I would mention, for example, section 51(a) which guarantees representation by provinces in this House of Commons; section 93 dealing with the right of provincial control over education; section 133 which deals with the right to use both the English and the French language in this parliament and in the courts. All these rights should be so entrenched that they could not be amended without the approval of the legislatures of all those provinces which might be affected.
To these rights should be added other fundamental rights which, unfortunately, are not embodied in our constitution and which I consider should be included before any process is finally accepted. I welcome and second the suggestion made by the hon. member for Royal that the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals, most of which are to be found in the present Canadian Bill of Rights should be incorporated in the fundamental document of our constitution. I am sure that if the Leader of the Opposition, one of the main proponents of the bill of rights, were in his place now he would acknowledge that they are not part of our constitution at the present time. The bill of rights is merely a statute of this parliament which can be amended by this parliament; it does not control the activities of the provinces in any way whatever. I therefore join in urging the Minister of Justice to include in the proposals to be made to the attorneys general of the provinces a proposal that incorporation of these fundamental rights in the constitution of Canada itself should take place.
But despite the fact that these fundamental provisions which I have enumerated-and there may be others to be added to them- should be entrenched in our constitution with a real degree of rigidity, there are many other provisions with respect to the distribution of powers between the provincial legislatures and the federal government which are of such a nature that they may well require amendment in the future, and these should be amendable by a consensus of the provinces and the federal parliament. For example, there is section 92(13) of the British North America Act which, as the committee knows, gives to the provincial legislatures legislative power over property and civil rights. In this phrase "property and

Supply-Justice
civil rights" there are no doubt included some purely local matters which particularly affect the local rights and cultures prevailing in individual provinces. But also included in this broad phrase "property and civil rights" are matters which from time to time require to be dealt with on the national level by the parliament of Canada if they are to be dealt with effectively at all. To give some illustrations, let me say there is a need for federal intervention so as to prevent fraudulent transactions in securities. Today the federal parliament has some dealing with this subject under the heading of the criminal law which falls within the federal power. There is also some provincial regulation. But there should be uniformity of legislation and administration across Canada in this regard. The hon. member for Royal has suggested this might well be done by delegation. I do not think we can rely on delegation. I believe an amendment is needed to deal with this problem.
Another aspect, one which is of urgent concern to farmers in particular, concerns the marketing of natural products. This, in some respects, is best suited to federal control especially with regard to commodities entering into export and import trade. Needed amendments in this field might well be prevented if there were a constitutional strait-jacket such as is involved in what I call the Fulton formula.
We are expecting almost momentarily to have revealed to us the long awaited national labour code. I would point out to the committee that this code will be a national labour code in name only; it will apply only to industries which fall under certain of the specific heads of federal jurisdiction set out in section 91. It does not apply to nationwide industries such as steel and packing houses, for example. At the moment provincial governments and their agencies are forced to try to cope on a provincial basis with problems which are national in scope.
Another important aspect of our affairs with regard to which amendments may be required in the future is lack of legislative power in respect to the implementation of international treaties. The federal power in this respect is seriously limited under the terms of our present constitution. Our successors

and perhaps some of us who are here today-may well find it necessary to amend the British North America Act so that Canada may have full power to carry out the international obligations it assumes.
These are merely illustrations of matters which might prove forever incapable of ade-

quate solution on a national scale if the inflexible form of amendment to the constitution is adopted. We all agree that the present provision for the amendment of the constitution is inadequate and out of date. We know that the only way to amend the constitution of Canada today, with the exception of certain matters covered by section 91(1) of the British North America Act, is by act of parliament of the United Kingdom. As long ago as 1926 the famous Balfour declaration was made after a conference, a commonwealth conference-I do not know whether they were called commonwealth conferences in those days. This declaration stated that the dominions were autonomous communities within the British empire equal in status and in no way subordinate to one another. We agree that since that day continuing reliance on the imperial parliament has been both anomalous and humiliating.
However, this form of amending process has at least one good thing to be said in its favour: It is flexible in its nature. It is a false and unwarranted doctrine that the British parliament would not act to amend the Canadian constitution without the consent of all the provinces. One just has to look at the recitals to the various amending acts to which the hon. member for Royal referred to see that in each case the act was passed by virtue of a resolution or request from the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada in parliament assembled. There are no references to seeking the consent of any of the provinces.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say that a suggestion that the British parliament would not pass any amendment to the constitution sought by the parliament of Canada is entirely without warrant; but-and this is the point I wish to make as clearly as I can- there is a grave danger that in removing this anomaly we will jump out of the frying pan into the fire. There is no reason at all why we should impose upon ourselves-and that is what we would be doing-the fetters of an unduly rigid amending procedure. The Fulton formula, as I see it, proposes this and even goes so far as to suggest that after we have locked ourselves up in this way we should throw away the key.
It is proposed that the amending formula, once it becomes law, can itself only be amended with the consent of all the provinces. I suggest that this is the doctrine of provincial rights run riot and it can only serve to destroy any truly workable federalism. After 100 years of living with a flexible

constitution, albeit one amendable in another country, are we, in the name of deliverance from national bondage, to impose upon ourselves absolute rigidity in regard to constitutional amendment?
It is my view, and I believe it is shared by a great many Canadians, that the pendulum is swinging too far toward the assertion of provincial rights. It is perfectly true that under our federal system provincial rights are vitally important, and there may still be many fields in which decentralization is important and required. I have tried to make it perfectly clear that in our view these fundamental provincial rights and minority rights should be entrenched beyond the possibility of amendment without the unanimous concurrence of all the provinces. But the imposition of a veto for every province upon constitutional amendment of any significance whatever would be a damaging blow to a truly workable federalism and Canada's status as a nation.
There are two other main observations that I would like to make. I would like to know who are the government's advisers on this particular matter, because I think they have been receiving poor advice. Has the government consulted those people in our universities, for example, who have made a study of amending procedures in Canada and throughout the world? I do not propose to detain the committee by analysing the amending procedures of other countries. I merely assert- and this I believe is a fact-that the particular form of amendment proposed in the so-called Fulton formula is unprecedented anywhere in the world.
I have examined the amending formula in Australia, for example, where after an absolute majority in each of the federal houses it must be submitted to a vote of electors in each state. If in a majority of states-let us say, four out of six-a majority of the voting electors approve and if a majority of all the voting electors approve, then the amendment will take effect. But the point is that this is far less rigid than the formula proposed for Canada; it is far less exacting. But even so, it has been complained of by many constitutional experts as being unduly restrictive in practice in Australia. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that we should have some witnesses from Australia to tell us how their amending formula is worked.
In the United States of America amendment may be proposed by a two thirds vote of both houses and ratified by the legislatures of three fourths of the states or by conven-
Supply-Justice
tions in three fourths of the states. I have mentioned Professor Bora Laskin, an eminent constitutional expert. He made a proposal which I suggest should be very seriously considered by the government, namely that with the exception of the entrenched clauses of the British North America Act which I have already mentioned, a proposal for amendment should become effective when initiated by a two thirds vote in the parliament of Canada and by a vote of the legislature in not less than two thirds of the provinces, provided the population of the approving provinces exceeds 50 per cent of the population of Canada. Such a formula would provide reasonable flexibility and at the same time ensure that amendments could not be made unless the general consensus across Canada approved of them. I have looked at the constitutions of West Germany and India; they likewise provide for a consensus rather than a simple majority, and they do not give to the smaller units making up the federations the right to veto constitutional changes.
The point which I wish to stress is that before any formula for amendment is adopted, the advice of experts should be listened to. I call the attention of the government and the committee to a resolution that was passed by the association of law teachers in June, 1961, when they were considering the proposed conference of attorneys general to establish procedures for the amendment of the Canadian constitution. They urged that the conference should be requested to establish a procedure for public hearings, at which submissions and representations on an amending procedure might be offered, and which would provide for investigation and report on other federal amending systems. They pointed out in their brief that this was a matter of fundamental importance to all Canadians; and I suggest it deserves to be considered, not with a hasty, hole-in-the-corner approach but should be afforded the widest possible publicity and the widest possible consultation with qualified people.
Lastly, Mr. Chairman, I wish to urge upon the government their responsibility in this matter. Constitutional reform in a great country such as Canada is not a matter of expedient policy at the moment; it is not something routine. Once it is adopted it is extremely hard to get away from. At the last conference a proposal was put forward by the federal government of the day which I have suggested, and others with more authority than I have, have stated, to be an unmitigated constitutional disaster. It seems to me that

Supply-Justice
this formula is a basic surrender on the part of the government of Canada to some exaggerated views on provincial rights.
At the former conference the government of Saskatchewan, advised I believe by Professor Frank Scott, the former dean of the law school of McGill and one of the foremost constitutional experts in this country, opposed this formula. The government of Saskatchewan has changed, and my view is that the government of that province is not now so well advised as it was previously. I suggest that it is the duty of the parliament of Canada and the government of Canada to ensure that in our haste to repatriate the constitution and end the anomaly of its control outside Canada we do not make the grievous error of hamstringing future Canadians in respect of their constitution. I believe it is high time that the government of Canada started to stand up for the rights of Canada as a whole and sounded a less uncertain note in respect of excessive claims of provincial rights. I suggest that this conference would be a very good place to start doing that.
The government should repudiate the so-called Fulton formula and produce something much closer to what I describe as the Laskin formula, although I am quite sure that Professor Laskin would be the last to claim originality or finality in his suggestions. I therefore urge that at the forthcoming conference the Minister of Justice, representing the government of Canada, do a number of things. I will list them, Mr. Chairman. (1) He should propose to the attorneys general a modified formula which would provide for the entrenchment of basic minority rights but would enable amendment in respect of other matters on the basis of a general provincial consensus. I have explained more in detail what I mean by that. (2) He should propose to the attorneys general of the provinces that simultaneously with the repatriation of the constitution there should be the incorporation of a bill of rights in the constitution; and (3) that he should urge upon the conference the adoption of the proposal of the association of law teachers, namely that there be adequate consultation and public hearing before any formula be determined. Only thus, in my view, will we be able to use the words of what I hope will some day be the official national anthem of Canada. Only thus will we in Canada and this parliament be able to say that we have stood on guard for Canada.

Mr. Chairman, could I ask the hon. member a question. I wonder whether he would elucidate this point of view. Does he
IMr. Brewin.]
consider the B.N.A. Act is a pact between the two founding nations, or an act which issued from a parliament which did not exist then?

This is a matter very much debated, Mr. Chairman. I would say, legally speaking, that it is not a pact but an act of parliament. But certainly I concur in the view that it was an act which embodied the nature of a basic agreement between different parts of Canada and should be respected as such.

May I put another question. Does he not consider that the question of the future majority vote in the house is destroying precisely the spirit of the pact itself, which proves it was an act and not a pact? If you consider the argument of the majority vote, you are referring to the original pact as the act of a parliament which did not exist.

I do not think the hon. member followed my proposal too carefully. I suggested that in addition to the two thirds vote of the parliament of Canada there should be the approval of seven out of the ten provinces representing at least 50 per cent of the population of Canada as a whole. I would point out to the hon. member that with that protection there would be reasonable flexibility; at the same time there would not be complete rigidity when any single province, no matter how small, could frustrate the general consensus among the people of Canada. I also hope the hon. member recognizes the point I made, that those fundamental rights with regard to education, religion, language and so on would be entrenched so that they could not be affected unless each one of the provinces agreed.
That is the letter but not the spirit of confederation.

Mr. Chairman, I regret that I am not able to make such a scholarly speech as the ones which we have just heard from the hon. members who preceded me and who are experienced jurists. However, I should like to say a few words, first in the name of my party, and then in my own name, as a citizen of the province of Quebec.
The position of our party concerning repatriation of the constitution is not yet quite definite, except that we are 100 per cent in favour of repatriation of this constitution and that we believe all the provinces are able, among themselves, to come to an understanding which will permit the realiza-

tion of this project in a friendly way and in a manner that can be accepted by the federal government.
Our party's attitude could be set out more specifically but, speaking as I do on behalf of our group, I shall limit myself to that statement of principle, because I am under the impression that we will have other opportunities this year to discuss this most important problem.
Mr. Chairman, a certain spirit was prevailing in Canada when, in 1867, a pact was signed by the various groups living in this country, but since we were not there, we do not know what that spirit was. However, anyone who does a little historical research will soon realize that it was some kind of spirit of compromise which was convenient for the parties concerned since, amongst other things, it enabled them to protect themselves against the immediate or remote possibility of invasion by the United States. The spirit which existed at that time must certainly have been such as I have just explained because, when things are considered logically, it is realized that, at the present time, Canada is a paradox, something irrational, anomalous and even absurd economically, socially and culturally. If Canada had wanted its own welfare, it could have made a decision at that time and I am convinced it would have decided to unite with our neighbours below the 45th parallel since, logically, it was an easy way to clear themselves of the prerogatives that had been granted their forefathers and which they had accepted. However, the citizens of the country decided otherwise. They decided to unite in a federation comprising various aspects which are considered more or less appropriate today.
If we listen to extremists, one side as well as the other, if we listen to those politicians who are interested in obtaining a vote rather than in settling a problem, it becomes obvious that the matter of repatriation of the constitution, just like the very existence of the confederation, is very complicated indeed. It should be divided into various points, but the participants always see it as a whole. Let me explain. The hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Valade) asked if it was a pact between two nations, between two founding groups, or if it was instead a federal law governing a group of provinces. Well, in my humble opinion, what happened in those days does not matter. I feel that it would be in order to differentiate between the union of two nations and that of two ethnic groups, or of
Supply-Justice
two founding groups or groups of provinces, which form part of this confederation. We cannot confuse both; we cannot say that the two equal groups must be dealt with on an equal footing. In my opinion, this is impossible from a human, geographical and even logical point of view. It is absolutely impossible to reach an understanding on a level of equality, because we are not equal.
On this point I would like to take issue with the comments the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) made when he spoke about Prince Edward Island. It is impossible to ask here that Prince Edward Island be treated on an equal footing with the rest of Canada. However, since the union of those provinces is a pact, or should be a pact, when the constitution is repatriated, or when it must be repatriated, then the provinces or the signatories of the pact must put forward their requests.
In the case of the province of Quebec, in 1864 and after that until 1867, when a confederation with the rest of the country was contemplated, the Quebec citizens were very reluctant, because they saw practically no advantage.
However, since it was at the same time a political action, the political leaders of that time decided to suggest a compromise which would be acceptable to the citizens of the province of Quebec as well as to the rest of the country.
That is why at that time mention was made of equality of languages, provincial control over education as well as a few other prerogatives granted to the provinces. Those were prerequisite conditions on the part of Quebec for a partnership in confederation.
If one considers the problem facing Prince Edward Island, one realizes that it was similar, without being identical. Prince Edward Island knew that because of its geographical situation and small population, it would be absorbed by the rest of the country if some particular points did not favour in a certain way, and perhaps at the expense of other areas of the country, the citizens of Prince Edward Island. In fact, it is only with the assurance and guarantee that those specific points would be granted them by the central government that the citizens of Prince Edward Island accepted to sign the agreement which resulted in confederation.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that one should not be, as suggested by the hon. member for Greenwood, a die-hard democrat. Specious arguments, such as the ones he advanced about proportional representation, should not

Supply-Justice
be accepted, because the same vital interests are not at stake. The vital interests of a province, or even of a city such as the one represented by the hon. member, may extend to a metropolis, a region, but when a country as extensive as Canada is concerned, one should not, in my opinion, confine oneself to the purest form of democracy, but to a logical argumentation liable to satisfy most if not all parties concerned.
Mr. Chairman, some time ago my opinion was sought on the concept of two nations. Even today a party colleague asked me the same thing. A few months ago, at the request of a newspaper representative, I wrote a brief article on this subject. It goes without saying that this is my personal opinion which may be shared, but not necessarily, by others. This is what I stated at that time:
This opinion is held by those in the van and, according to the reaction of the Anglo-Saxon group, it might well be prevalent in a few years. Should it so happen, it would most surely meet with the approval of the majority of French speaking Quebeckers.
As for me, I feel that both nations should be fully recognized on the federal level. With regard to the relations which should exist between the various part of Canada now called "provinces", I feel our concept of the matter should change.
I could easily see, in order to foster economic integration, the forming of five zones which, for practical purposes, could replace the provinces. These new economic zones would be: the maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario, the prairie provinces and the western provinces.
It is only under conditions of this type that the concept of two nations across Canada could really be considered as a possibility.
It must be obvious, Mr. Chairman, that I make a very clear distinction between the different objectives sought, at the present time, by the various provinces in confederation.
I can quite understand why all Liberal members are sometimes astonished by the attitude taken by the province of Quebec. As a matter of fact, we from the province of Quebec are astonished by the attitude taken, for instance, by Premier Lesage, which is contradictory to the lines he defended when he was in this house and when he was fighting for a political party rather than for an ideology. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I am convinced that today political interests have a more important bearing upon the opinions expressed by our leaders in Quebec than the specific interest of the province itself. At this moment it is great to be approved by certain newspapers, certain groups of intellectuals, certain pressure groups or even by extremists who are found mostly among teen-agers and students, who

are a political capital which must be tended to in view of an electoral campaign.
A federal election campaign?

A provincial election campaign. However, when it comes to setting out clearly Quebec's needs and demands, it is often obvious that even politicians find it hard to explain them or at a loss to do so. That is why we, of the province of Quebec, sometimes witness reversals of opinion which can only be explained by a certain amount of political ambition.
These remarks are not intended as a criticism. It is just that the more experience I get about politics, the more I realize that one has to have a minimum of ambition to remain in politics. Be that as it may, when the problems involved are as consequential as the ones we are dealing with now, I feel that the people of Canada should at least be told about them so that they may form an opinion as to Quebec's demands.
Mr. Chairman, earlier the hon. member for Greenwood spoke about the unanimity of decisions as it is set forth in the so-called Fulton bill. I have here the Fulton bill which does not seem quite in agreement with the opinions expressed by the hon. member for Greenwood.
It is said in that bill, that under certain circumstances, in order to amend legislation existing at present in the provinces, or the legislation or privileges granted to those provinces by our constitution the agreement of all the provinces will be necessarily required.
Section 3 of part I provides that when a piece of legislation affects one province more than another, or affects only one group of provinces, excluding others, it cannot come into effect without the consent of the legislature of each province to which that provision applies.
In my opinion this is a very useful concession made to the provinces which would like to take advantage of it.
When he speaks of the majority of the provinces and of at least 50 per cent of the population, he is merely referring to section (5) of the same part 1 of the Fulton bill which states-I shall skip some of the details of the clause-that no law enacted under the present part shall be put into force without the co-operation of at least two thirds of the provincial legislatures, which represent at least 50 per cent of the Canadian population, according to the last general census.

Thus, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that these guarantees are sufficient to enable all the provinces, including Ontario, to sign a new confederation agreement or to agree to the constitution being repatriated.
When he speaks of the rights of the minorities I do not know to what rights he is referring. As far as I am concerned I have never recognized, and I still do not recognize, French Canada or French Canadians as being a minority.
At this point I should like to quote an opinion expressed by Mr. Eugene Forsey, who happens to be very friendly with the group of the hon. member for Greenwood. He said this:
The actual recognition of the French partner is the price we pay to preserve Canada and if the English majority is not willing to pay that price, it is because fundamentally it does not really want a united Canada.
Personally, Mr. Chairman, I endorse this statement of a prominent English speaking Canadian and I point out that as far as minorities are concerned, any minority might be mentioned except the French Canadians. French Canadians are not a minority group. As I said earlier, their group must be on the same footing as the other one on the federal and the cultural level, maybe not necessarily on the economic level, because this is a field that comes under provincial jurisdiction and does not concern the ethnic group itself.
But the ethnic group in itself is equal to any other group in Canada, it cannot be considered as a minority.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, it seems that Quebec's position is somewhat contradictory. In certain cases, however, it should be recognized that its claims are well founded.
The French Canadian group should not be recognized as a minority, but it is. Let us say that there is a French group and an English group in Canada and let us consider both as such, irrespective of their number. One realizes that they form what could be called monolithic blocks. We have two groups with different aspirations, a different conception of problems, and the conclusions they draw from their arguments are also different. This means that of 19 million inhabitants, 14 million think the same way, consider problems from the same point of view, while on the other hand, 5 million consider problems from an entirely different point of view.
As it will always be the same thing and as the only protection that the French speaking people could have with regard to maintaining their way of thinking and the concepts they
Supply-Justice
consider in their best interest, this group wants a written guarantee in the constitution to the effect that the majority will never be able to impose any decision against the will of French Canadians.
This would explain the claims made from time to time by the representatives of the province of Quebec.
But there has been some proof, even quite recently, that it was quite easy to get around those claims in a dialogue with Quebec. When, as was stated just now, it was a matter of unemployment insurance, old age pensions, student loans, some agreement was always reached at the end of a discussion, which was perhaps not quite constitutional nor in keeping with the policy established in 1867, but which seemed satisfactory to everybody, to every province, to Quebec as well as to the federal government.
To my mind the decisions taken at that time tend to show that the province of Quebec has an open mind and is ready to co-operate. But this open mind wants, none the less, to maintain the standards for which it has fought over the years.
As I said, the reason why Quebec does not so much want concessions, but written terms incorporated in a statute, is simply the wish to have an additional guarantee and to be more particularly assured that, even if the good people of this parliament should disappear, whichever government be in power and whatever the scientific and ideological training of those who will succeed them, this guarantee will always have a place in a legal text accepted by the parties to the covenant.
Mr. Chairman, when a pact is signed by two parties and one decides to change some clauses of that pact, if it is intended that the pact be redrafted and that an agreement be possible, this agreement must necessarily exist between the two contracting parties.
If, in 1964, the province of Quebec entertains aspirations and demands different from those of 1867, it has the right to say so and refuse to sign a new contract as long as its demands are not met.
That is the reason why separatism exists at present. It is because the people of Quebec think that, if the other contracting party will not accede to the wishes of the French Canadian group, the latter will not sign or renew a confederation pact. Consequently, it will withdraw from confederation, or rather confederation will be formed without the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, I would not like to go any further today. I just wanted to try to explain

Supply-Justice
certain stands taken by the province of Quebec. I repeat, I am not speaking on behalf of my party but in my own name.
However, there is one thing which must not be forgotten and which I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, namely that Canada is in itself a paradox, if we consider it in the light of the presence of the United States. It is a complete paradox. While trade patterns are usually from north to south we have decided that they would be, in our case, from east to west; we have decided, with certain difficulties, to control a certain part of our economy; we are trying our utmost to live in a state of nearly continuous heroism simply because we want to maintain our own entity.
I think this is normal, and it is a very good thing for this country, Canada, to continue in the same direction. Otherwise, it would only have to lean toward the United States.
If this paradox is accepted, then the one concerning French presence within confederation must also be accepted, and you must accept that, while it will cost a little more, while there are a few more annoyances, while it is necessary in certain cases to make the debate a little heavier, we must continue to accept this paradox. It is the sine qua non condition for a persistent confederation, and I think that it will be one of the only reasons which will allow the celebration of the centennial of our Canadian confederation.

Mr. Chairman, I should be vexed with myself if I did not join at this stage in the debate announced on Monday by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), when he stated, as reported on page 8524 of Hansard:
On Wednesday, in order to give members of this house an opportunity to express their views in respect of amendments to the constitution of Canada being made in Canada, I intend to have the estimates of the Department of Justice placed before the house, but only for that purpose.
He was referring in the end to the possibility of discussing the amending or repatriation of the constitution governing at present Canada as a whole.
While the Minister of Justice announced the business of the house last night, I studied a statement made by one of his good friends, Frangois Aquin of the "Federation liberale du Quebec''.
An old acquaintance.

An old acquaintance, as the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger), who is hiding behind the curtains says.

The Minister of Justice, and the other members, became acquainted yesterday with Mr. Aquin's statement to the effect that he considers co-operative federalism as a formula to amend the Canadian constitution, a mere electoral "gadget".
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Justice champions the cause of co-operative federalism in the province of Quebec. When he speaks on co-operative federalism to the workers in his constituency, the latter understands neither the "a", nor the "z", nor the "b" of it.
That is true.
That is true. What is cooperative federalism-
And Social Credit?

I hear my hon. friend from St. Maurice-Lafleche say "Social Credit". If he learned about it perhaps he would be reasoning differently from the way he is now reasoning in the strait-jacket put on him by the Liberal party.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. What the member for Villeneuve has just said-
Come now, there is no question of privilege.
Order; the hon. member for Villeneuve has the floor.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think we have to be taught any lesson by anyone opposite; on the other hand, I could teach them one.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Chairman, for many months we have been hearing so much about co-operative federalism that people in the east or in the west do not understand anything about it. I would be remiss at this stage if I did not put on the record the exact meaning of co-operative federalism, according to my interpretation and according to people who understand something about it.
Co-operative federalism would consist of federal-provincial plans at all levels of administration, at all levels of the Canadian economic activity, which means a participation of the provincial and federal governments to all kinds of plans, in such fields as health, highways, the trans-Canada highway,

the seaway, etc. Everywhere the federal and the provincial government would be involved. As far as I am concerned that is the meaning of co-operative federalism.
That is why Mr. Aquin was perfectly right when he said that co-operative federalism was only an election gadget.
And as my good friend the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) just suggested, the minister of natural resources of the province of Quebec stated that co-operative federalism is the abortion of the French Canadian nation in Canada. I think that the Minister of Justice agrees with the minister of natural resources on that. It is a fact. This would be the abortion or simply the elimination of French Canadians in Canada.
As the hon. member for Quebec-Montmor-ency (Mr. Marcoux) just said, French Canadians of the province of Quebec are not asking anything from others. It is an actual fact and if our Anglo-Saxon friends are not aware of it, they will realize it by seeing us in action. They simply ask for the opportunity and the privilege to develop as they see fit. We are not asking the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice or any other minister to grant us favours at the expense of others. No. We are simply asking for the right to act according to our views, our culture, our possibilities, our ability, in order to develop our part of the country called the province of Quebec, and nothing else.
There are always some sly ones who travel through Canada saying that Quebec wants to take away this or that from other provinces, that Quebec claims too much, and this and that, when they do not know the first thing about Quebec. As for us, we know what Quebec is. I am the first one to say, not only to the other provinces, but to my own province of Quebec, that if it is true that economically speaking we are lagging behind the other Canadian provinces, the English speaking people in Toronto, Winnipeg or Vancouver are certainly not to blame, and it is rather the fault of French Canadians in Quebec who, instead of serving their Canadian homeland, have been promoting partisanship ever since confederation in 1867.
Hail Duplessis.

My hon. friend says "Hail Duplessis". What does he know about Duplessis? He has never met him in his life because Duplessis is dead. My hon. friend may die in the same way.
Supply-Justice
I am sorry I met you.

Listen to what I am saying and you will understand that the French Canadians in the province of Quebec are not asking you for any favours. We are just asking for justice for our province, as you are asking for justice for your province.
He is narrow-minded; never mind him.
Do not get excited.

Do not throw Duplessis into the picture; Duplessis is not here today.

Mr. Chairman, we have had enough of those ill-willed interjections neither intelligible nor intelligent, on the part of people who do not even understand what is going on in the province of Quebec as well as in the other provinces. I say to my hon. friend, who comes from British Columbia, that if there are people who have at heart the development of the province of Quebec, there are others also who care very much for the development of the province of British Columbia, in spite of the C.C.F. and socialism which prevent Social Crediters from working in this regard at the present time, but who nevertheless succeed in spite of all that.
You had better get back to your text.

Do not interrupt me, then, and I will get back. I do not need to have a text. I can tell you without a text exactly what I think of what you are saying just now.

For many years now, Mr. Chairman, we have been hearing about co-operative federalism from various members of the government. We also hear of the repatriation of the Canadian constitution. I wonder if the Minister of Justice knows where that constitution is hidden. Everybody has been searching for it during the last ten years but nobody can find it. Is it hidden on some shelves?
It is under the table. [Translation]
Yes, under the table.

Is it in the London parliament? We do not know, and in this corner of the house we say: why rack your brains in trying to repatriate something which has never been accepted by the Canadian people?

Supply-Justice
Mr. Chairman, let us leave the constitution where it is. Do we need to go to London to know what we the elected members of parliament, the representatives of the people, must or can do here in Canada? Let us ignore the old constitution of 1864 or 1867.
I would like here to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice on this point. Let us leave that constitution to England and let us elaborate a new Canadian constitution, one that will take into account the current economic, political and social facts in Canada, the possibilities, the potential at all levels, in all respects, in this country.
But no, instead of adapting a truly Canadian constitution to the needs of the time, for a number of years it has been proposed to repatriate a constitution with which nobody is acquainted. This constitution, which, after all, is only an act of the British parliament, was never submitted to the approval of the Canadian people, and today, everybody agrees, Conservatives as well as Liberals, members of the New Democratic party, members of the Social Credit party and we the members of the Ralliement Creditistes, that this act has become obsolete and even prejudicial to the economic development of our country, to its sovereignty.
Mr. Chairman, under this ancient constitution, the intrusion of the federal government in the fields reserved to the provinces has become intolerable. For instance, in the field of education, we saw recently the government introduce legislation intended to help university students through loans of $1,000 per annum for a period of five years. The federal government is trying to invade the field of education.
Where highways are concerned, there is the trans-Canada highway. Where agriculture is concerned, the Minister of Agriculture plans federal grants to the provinces, whereas the provinces themselves should handle their program of grants to help agriculture. And in many other fields of our economy, of our economic activity, the federal government tries to interfere to assert its authority as we have seen recently. That is why I maintain that instead of manipulating, I repeat "manipulating", a constitution which is unfamiliar to us, which is in London, we should let London play around with the constitution of 1867 and work out our own constitution of 1964.
On the other hand there are people like the prime minister of Quebec, Mr. Lesage, who state, as he did in he Devoir of September 29 last, that, in brief, the two nations must be equal, and that the political frame-
[Mr. Caouette.l
work of Quebec should be provided with all the means required to develop the French Canadian nation. Not to the prejudice of the English Canadian nation, no, but to give to Quebec economical and political standards and provide it with all the necessary means to ensure the development of the French Canadian nation.
Today, right-thinking people throughout the country accept such a solution, but Mr. Lesage stated yesterday, September 29: "It is too early to discuss changes to be effected to our constitution", while his colleague, Mr. Rene Levesque said: "We are late", and his colleague, Mr. Aquin: "The Minister of Justice is presenting us with an electoral gadget" and Mr. Gerin-Lajoie maintains: "The time has come to amend the constitution."
Mr. Chairman, the premier of the province of Quebec stated yesterday: It is first of all a question of the French Canadians having a status equal in all respects to that of the English Canadians. Some people will surely object. I have met provincial premiers both in western Canada and eastern Canada who claimed: "Quebec is only one of the ten provinces." That is not the spirit of the confederation pact of 1867, which clearly set out the equality of the two groups who signed that pact the French and the English. In my opinion, French speaking Canadians have held up their end of the bargain. French should become a working language within the federal civil service and be taught everywhere one finds a French speaking minority. My English speaking friends must admit, regardless of party affiliation, that there are no such school, municipal or provincial problems in Quebec between the French and the English. In the province of Quebec, the English speaking people definitely form a minority, but they enjoy the same legislation, the same privileges and the same treatment granted to the clear majority of French Canadians. We have no trouble in Montreal, in Sherbrooke, in Quebec city nor in Rouyn-Noranda between both groups. English speaking Protestants and French speaking Roman Catholics get the same grants from the government. McGill University, proportionally, gets even more than Montreal university.
Mr. Chairman, there is no discrimination in the province of Quebec; why should there be elsewhere?
Why are attempts made elsewhere to disparage French Canadians from Quebec, when in Quebec, we do not discriminate against our English friends?

In my own constituency there is a large number of English speaking people. However, we do not quarrel and there is no discrimination against them. Why should it be otherwise in Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia and in the maritimes against French Canadian minorities?
When Mr. Lesage says: "To have French become a working language in the federal government and a language taught everywhere else where French minorities are found", he is voicing our hope.
In fact, for a long time now, three sessions, we have been claiming for the French minorities in the other provinces exactly the same treatment which is granted the English minority in Quebec.
According to Le Devoir of September 29, 1964, Mr. Lesage stated:
Second, French Canada demands a true decentralization of powers, of resources and of decision centres within the federal system: "Quebec, as I have often said (this is Mr. Lesage speaking), believes in the harmony created through consultation and discussion among equals, and not in the harmony which stems from uniformity imposed by an all-powerful central government.
No co-operative federalism, according to Mr. Lesage. I continue:
At the present time we believe that our political structures are sufficiently flexible, particularly if they are adapted to present circumstances, to enable all the means required for the development of the French Canadian nation concentrated within our borders to be centralized at the level of the Quebec government. These political structures, based on historic, geographic and economic facts, are sufficiently strong to ensure the continued existence of a country extending from sea to sea.
And Quebec will never avoid its obligations or the assistance it wants to give national understanding, to create a climate of national unity within the framework of our country, Canada. Quebec has never avoided its obligations.
Mr. Chairman, I have here the report of the Quebec economic advisory council. This report contains, not only concerning the province of Quebec but the whole country, a few directions concerning the Canadian constitution which, we hope, will be submitted to us as soon as the Minister of Justice will have conferred with provincial premiers or with representatives of provincial governments. In its report, the Quebec economic planning council expresses the following opinion:
The Quebec government has no control at present on certain important instruments of economic control.
(a)	Currency; to the extent that economic activity depends on the existence of a universally accepted medium, such activity is under the exclusive control of the federal government. Since the central govern-
