ment has the authority to issue currency, (through the Bank of Canada, necessarily), or to control the variations of the money supply in circulation, it exerts a direct control on inflation (and on deflation at the same time) on the revalorization or the loss of value of currency itself.
The public or private debt of Quebec abroad, the long term commitments of Quebeckers to foreigners, may therefore change considerably, without the government of Quebec having anything to do with it.
We saw it illustrated when the authorities of the city of Montreal borrowed the amount of $60 million in the United States, in order to build a subway section. It is impossible to find the required financing within the limits of the province of Quebec, and then people come and tell us that this province is free.
I continue reading from the report:
(b)	Customs tariffs:	The government of the
province has no right to keep a market for any industry by means of customs tariffs. On the other hand, the economic entity, which the province represents, may be seriously affected by the right exercised in this case by the government of Canada, for instance, where high tariffs protect an important product which is manufactured in Canada but which is not or cannot, for some reason, be produced in Quebec.
(c)	Taxation: The constitution grants the province the right to collect only direct taxes. But this right also belongs to the government of Canada. The two governments share the tax potential with regard to their respective needs.
And that is where we can see the wonderful spectacle of double taxation in the province of Quebec.
And the report says further:
Historically speaking, the taxes collected by the Canadian government have increased much more rapidly than those collected by the government of Quebec, more particularly because of war, so that, at this time, the government of the province collects a minor part (16 per cent in 1962) of the total tax paid by individuals, and 22 per cent of corporation taxes, against 84 per cent and 78 per cent respectively collected by the government of Canada, excluding equalization payments. This distribution prevails, whereas taxes of all kinds have reached an unprecedented level, and its practical consequence is to freeze the freedom of the province of Quebec theoretically empowered to meet its needs directly. These needs exceed the revenues by far and are growing at a rate which increases steadily.
Mr. Chairman, as may be seen by reading the following article, the Creditistes are not the only ones to speak about credit control. In fact, the Quebec economic advisory council states in its report:
We are speaking here of the establishment of credit as an extension of the money instrument. To the degree where the economic activity depends on credit control by the Canadian banking system and to the extent where such a system is liable to

Supply-Justice
be controlled, such activity is influenced only by the action of the government of this country (Ottawa) on the banks.
Here, as in taxation matters, the views of the Canadian government are not necessarily attuned to the evolution of a given regional economic unit. Such consideration applies particularly to the province of Quebec, the rate of expansion of which should henceforth be accelerated in comparison to the rest of the country.
The government of the province of Quebec can, however, remedy its present lack of control on the economy by taking initiatives likely to help it or the province of Quebec develop.
Mr. Chairman, before concluding my remarks, and as I pointed out at the beginning, I should recall that the province of Quebec requests no favours from the others. But we, the members of the Creditistes, in the light of the social credit theory, have asked for a change, improvements or amendments to the constitution.
We proposed four points. First, that the control of credit be given to the province.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has run out. However, he may continue his remarks if the house agrees.
Mr. Chairman, I need only two minutes.
Go on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps the house would agree to give a few minutes to the hon. member, so that he may conclude his remarks.
Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, I am grateful to my excellent friends for allowing me to conclude my remarks. Besides, I shall be very brief.
I want to mention what the Ralliement Creditiste suggested on January 26, 1964, in the light of the principles of the Social Credit.
First, give back to the provinces the control of credit. If it is called branches of the Bank of Canada in each province, we are in favour, but let the Bank of Canada help the provinces, or the province, to the extent of the development wanted by the province.
Credit should not be a hindrance to the economic development of a province, whether it is Quebec, Ontario or any other Canadian province.
Second, control of foreign and domestic trade, of imports and exports, namely what we sell to foreign countries in raw or manufactured materials.

Instead of selling the province of Quebec iron ore or instead of giving it to the Americans, as we are now doing, why not process that product in a new steel industry, in a secondary industry which would be set up in the province in order to sell finished products to the Americans, instead of selling them a raw material which they process and sell back to us as a finished product? Thus, American workers are benefiting from the natural resources of the province of Quebec and of Canada as a whole.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, we should control our imports and exports to know what goes out of the province and what comes in.
Third, the return of fiscal rights-I see the Minister of Justice is taking notes- of direct taxation which in any case belong to the provinces. Let us give unto the provinces that which belongs to them. We know, and the Minister of Justice is also aware of the fact, that it was the war which brought us to accept the federal government's intrusion into provincial fields of taxation. The rights the provinces granted the federal government should have been given back to them right after the war in 1945, or 20 years ago, but the federal government are still playing around in fields of taxation which normally, and according to the constitution, belong to the provinces.
Fourth, control over immigration. This does not mean that Quebec should stop Ukrainians, Poles, Italians or Irish immigrants from coming into the province, not at all, but the thing is to know who is going to come to our province.
Quebec has citizens of Polish origin, Ukrainian origin, indeed, people of all nationalities which are the pride of our province. However, it is painful for us to hear someone say to a Ukrainian at Wolfe's Cove, in Quebec city: "If you wish to earn a living in Canada, you must learn English instead of French."
Personally, I was glad to learn English and I readily advise those who do not know the language to learn it, but I would say to any foreigner who comes to Quebec: Start by learning French, since it is the language of the majority in this province. Afterwards you may learn English as a third language." That would make me happy.
I wish to know who comes into Quebec and who moves out. A number of French Canadians from the province of Quebec have left their homeland and gone to the United

States and thousands of French Canadians are going to that country in order to earn a living.
Why, Mr. Chairman, are our people leaving this country to go to the United States? Because they And it difficult to earn a decent and honourable living in the province of Quebec.
Let us begin by creating economic conditions that will enable the Canadian workers as a whole, the Quebec citizens as a whole to earn their living in their own province, in their own country, in Canada. Then, I feel that we will have been very useful to our Canadian people, of whatever origin they may be.
I am saying this, Mr. Chairman, merely to state our position as regards the repatriation of the Canadian constitution, that has been in the dark since 1867.
We are in 1964 and in three years we shall reach 1967. As I said at the outset of my remarks-and I call the attention of the Minister of Justice to that point-let us forget about the old constitution and let us work out a 1964 Canadian constitution that each and every Canadian, of English, French, Ukrainian, Polish or Italian origin, will find it possible to earn a living in his country and to make Canada one of the most prosperous countries in the whole world.
Carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I just heard someone say "Carried". I do not want to disappoint my own colleagues and members of my party; it was probably meant to be a joke. I simply wish to remind that today's debate is but the beginning of a general discussion on item 1 of the estimates of my department and that it will resume fully when the estimates will be again before the house, in a fortnight.
I wish to insist upon what I said earlier today; in view of the conference of attorneys general which will be held shortly, in view of the fact that I am president of that conference and also chief of the Canadian delegation, I do not think that it would be appropriate for me to take part in a discussion on this matter.
I wish to seize this opportunity to thank the hon. members who took part in today's debate. In clarifying and expressing the ideas which stem from their former research, they doubtless have given me and the cabinet some information which will help shape the policies of the government at the forthcoming conference.
Supply-Justice

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I could ask the minister a question before he sits down. What procedure does the government intend to follow with reference to these discussions with the provinces regarding the repatriation of the constitution? The reason I ask the question is that there has been a growing tendency during both last session and this session for the federal and provincial government to reach certain agreements and then for the federal government to bring them back to parliament. Members of parliament thus find themselves very much in the position of rubber stamps. These agreements have already been made and we are told from time to time that they cannot be altered because they have already been agreed upon with the provinces, and that it is impossible to go back to the provinces and ask them to change their position.
I think the minister is to be commended for giving this committee the opportunity today to express the views of the different parties with respect to the amending procedure in connection with the constitution, but will there be any opportunity for this matter to come back so that we know what is the thinking of the federal government, and what proposals they intend to pursue with the provinces? Or rather, is it the minister's thought that this matter will not come back to parliament until after an agreement has been signed, sealed and delivered, parliament then having no opportunity to do other than to accept or to reject it? It seems to me that this is placing parliament in a fairly difficult position, and I am wondering whether the minister can tell us what procedure he intends to follow in pursuing this matter of the constitutional discussions with the provincial governments.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think I have fairly well stated the position which, at least at the initial stage of the conference, the government intend to take by limiting myself to a reading of the official communique issued by the Prime Minister and the premiers at the last conference in Charlottetown. It is quite clear that at this stage all of the parties, including the federal government, have agreed that the Fulton formula, as it has been called, Mr..Fulton being chairman of the conference at the time, which was achieved as a result of very serious and lengthy negotiations between the delegates of the provincial governments and the federal government, be accepted in principle as the basis for the discussions.

Supply-Justice
It is a known fact that in 1961 at least three of the provinces, for different reasons, stated that they did not wish to agree to the formula as reflected in the draft act submitted to them by their respective attorneys general unless they had an occasion to discuss the possibility of certain clarifications being made in respect of paragraph 1, section 91 of the British North America Act. All I can say at the moment is this, that these conferences have shown in the past that they are meetings where in fact a series of earnest attempts have been made to negotiate a formula for the repatriation of the constitution and subsequent amendment, which would be acceptable to the provincial and federal governments.
The conference which is called for Monday has been called for the purpose of attempting to finalize, or "suggest" would perhaps be more precise, to these prime ministers and premiers who will be reunited in a subsequent conference, a formula which might be acceptable to their respective governments. In other words, it is not the purpose of the conference of the attorneys general to finalize a formula and come to an agreement which would be a fait accompli. Certainly I am not authorized in that regard. Our mandate, as reflected in the communique of the Charlottetown conference, is to discuss the formula and then report on our discussion to the conference of the prime ministers, which will be called I believe for October 13, after the Queen's visit.
The prime ministers' conference, of course, is under the responsibility of the Prime Minister of Canada, and under his chairmanship, and I would prefer that any technical aspects as to procedures to be followed be discussed by him and reported on to the members of this house by him. If I were to state a procedure prior to the conference which I am charged with chairing, I think I would be exceeding the limits of my own function as the Minister of Justice. My only authority is to find out what are the suggestions, to attempt to be instrumental in arriving at a formula which I hope the conference will be able to report to the conference of prime ministers.

I wonder whether I may be permitted to ask a further question, Mr. Chairman? This question was asked by the hon. member for Royal, but does the minister anticipate that this will accomplish anything beyond making the constitution a Canadian document? Is there any change in

substance in the B.N.A. Act to be discussed at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
As I stated a few minutes ago, certain provinces, particularly the province of Quebec, have stated that they wish to discuss possible modifications to section 91, paragraph 1 which, as you know, concerns the power of amending the constitution in Canada. That is the reason why certain governments would not accept the 1961 formula. I must say that this will be one of the factors involved in shaping the procedure of the conference. To date I have received no correspondence from the attorney general of any province concerning specific modifications which he has been requested to propose. I can visualize, therefore, that what will happen is what is common to this type of conference. Once the respective instructions given by the various provinces to their attorneys general have been set out at the opening of this conference, we will then know for sure what formula will be proposed. All of us in this house know that during these conferences various formulae are suggested at the commencement of the discussions, and then modified by the changing of a word or a principle. It is only after the conclusion of such a conference that we really are in a position to report on the collective position.
I should like to repeat, and I take responsibility for these remarks as being my own firm viewpoint, that it would be contrary to the best interests of such a conference, which was being carried out in earnest and with all frankness, that any of the parties should take a public firm position. It is my opinion that if the situation were otherwise it would be very difficult to have discussions which would proceed on a smooth basis and in a way likely to prove fruitful.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask one other question? As I understood the minister, the only question beyond the formula that might be considered would be a question in respect of section 91(1), which in itself relates to amending the constitution. Would the minister agree with me that this is one subject he has mentioned, and really does not have anything to do with changing of provincial and federal powers, but merely relates to amending the constitution itself? I understand the conference will only deal with a procedure to bring the constitution home and will not discuss any matters of substance as between the federal and provincial governments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows in this respect, there are conflicting views as to whether or not section 91 (1) ought to be part of an amending formula, or whether or not it is part of an amending formula. I know these views have been well expressed in the past, but the hon. member will also remember that in 1961 Ontario and Quebec at least felt that this was part of an amending formula.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Edmonton West.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit me one question? May I ask the Minister of Justice if up to this point there have been any discussions, or whether it is planned to have any discussions, on the way in which the final act would be taken, provided agreement on a formula and agreement on repatriating the constitution are reached? If I may put my question in another form, is it planned that the final act giving us authority over our own affairs will be taken by the parliament of the United Kingdom or will it be effected by an enacting body in this country, or perchance both? I am not asking for a decision on the matter; I am asking whether this phase of the matter is being discussed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must be very frank and say that in view of the background of the conference I have not considered that this particular subject would be one to be discussed at the conference of the attorneys general, because my view is that the conference of attorneys general at least will be concerned exclusively with the contents of the amending formula and not so much with the procedure of repatriation. I know my hon. friend has very personal and firm views on the possibility, once an amending formula has been devised, of making some kind of declaration or taking some kind of legislative action in parliament to state that henceforth this is the constitution of Canada. If I were to state my own personal views at present on this point I would say that I think it would be preferable that that particular thing be done as the last and final amendment to the constitution by the United Kingdom parliament, the authority which originally enacted the constitution as a statute reflecting an agreement between the provinces, rather than doing it the other way. But I must say I am very ready to consider the matter and to raise the point at the con-
Supply-Justice
ference as it has been raised by my hon. friend. This once more goes to show how useful these discussions are.

Mr. Chairman, my short intervention this afternoon will not be made under any pretence of being an expert in constitutional law. While the discussion this afternoon has been inhibited from the point of view of a free exchange of ideas by the fact that the Minister of Justice indicated that he felt it would be rather difficult for him to disclose the bargaining position of the federal government at the forthcoming conference of attorneys general at this time, yet there have been indications of some ideas from the other side of the house. I do not think the debate has been as full as one would have hoped, and I think the minister will agree with me that if ideas have been advanced it has been a rather one-sided affair. After all, the present situation has prevented a free flow of ideas and to this extent the circumstances surrounding this afternoon's discussion are relevant.
With regard to what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, it seems to me that this is only one more indication that we are far from being out of the woods in this connection. I think the best that can be said of the Charlottetown conference is that there was agreement on the desirability of repatriating the Canadian constitution, provided an appropriate formula could be found, and I put it to hon. members that the forthcoming conference is designed precisely for that purpose. In other words, its purpose is to find a vehicle or formula whereby there will be complete agreement on the formula under which the constitution may be repatriated.
But there is a further stumbling block, and I use that term perhaps because of a deficiency of our language. However, one of the obstacles or stages in the repatriation of the constitution involves the precise point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as to what the method shall be as distinct from the formula, because there again there may be opportunity for disagreement. I hope not, but certainly we must not go into this matter starry-eyed and oblivious of certain of the pitfalls that surround such a difficult course of negotiations.
As I said, I feel that so far there has been a generally expressed desire to repatriate the constitution. There are two points of view. One is that we will get it home and then we will discuss the situation afterwards. In other words, it is said that the big objective is to

Supply-Justice
get the constitution back in Canada and then we will look around and see what changes have to be made. This course has certain inherent dangers in that if the formula for amendment is not worked out beforehand and the constitution is brought home to Canada we may find ourselves, as has been said rather frequently, in a strait-jacket with no possibility of movement. I think it is also conceivable that consent to import or repatriate the constitution may be made a bargaining point with regard to the price for certain changes advanced by certain of the provinces. I say certain of the provinces, but the federal government might also be in the same position.
After all, so far most of the emphasis has been placed on changes to be insisted upon by one segment of Canada, the province of Quebec. I deny that emphasis because I think the situation goes far beyond that. In the evolution of Canada to the mid-1960's I think we have failed to recognize that in far too many sectors of the country there has been an evolution into regional developments, and in my opinion it is a mere illusion to think that we will be able to fashion a project of law that will affect all regions equally. There are regional interests, and when one province insists it is not a province like the others I say yes, but so are others different too. This is becoming more and more so. I suggest to hon. members that this is occurring in the evolution or the growth of this nation. Our coasts run from between 400 or 500 and 5,000 miles. I must not forget my hon. friends from the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. I am sure they are going to have some pertinent questions to put to the minister as to where they are going to fit into this picture on the repatriation of the constitution. We must remember that we come from existing provinces, but these hon. members come from potential provinces and I think they have a right to be heard at this time. These regional changes must be taken into account. I think allowance must be made for them. Anyone who denies them, I think, has a rather parochial outlook in so far as the development of Canada is concerned.
Now, I do not want to go into any discussion of the merits, demerits or difficulties connected with any of the proposed formulas. Reference has been made to the so-called Fulton formula, which has certain proponents in this house as well as critics, such as the hon. member for Greenwood. However, I leave that to people who have made a deeper study of constitutional law.

However, there is one point in connection with the relationship between the federal government and the provinces, and between the provinces themselves, which should be discussed when these changes which must be made are discussed. I refer to trade barriers. I would put it to the minister that I think this is going to be part of the price of the conference, if not this one then the next one or possibly the third conference, before we are in a position to say that we have agreed. This is something which is becoming much more pronounced and is something which I consider to be, if not a breach of the letter, certainly a breach of the spirit of the constitution. As I have said, I refer to infringements on the free flow of trade between provinces. We have seen all sorts of incidents of this type, and they are always put on a special basis. There are always laudatory motives and good reasons such as the encouragement of industry.
I would put it to hon. members, however, that in so doing these provincial administrations-and this goes for municipal administrations as well-frankly are in breach of the spirit of the constitution in that they are imposing, perhaps not directly, but some of them almost directly, barriers to the free flow of trade between the provinces. I am not going to name names or I am not going to cite particular incidents because this would identify these so-called governments. There are practices such as allowing certain bonuses to tenderers if the products are made in certain provinces or if the tenderers are operating businesses within a province, and I think those practices are wrong from the national point of view. All you are doing is gouging out your neighbour's eyes, and hoping that you will profit thereby. I do not believe you are the gainer. You may be the temporary gainer, but if your neighbour loses his eye in the process what gain have you made, if both of you are united in a common cause for the development of this country? I cannot see it. These practices are being multiplied left, right and centre. I for one cannot see how by the manipulation of sales tax levels, credits and perhaps some other proposals for certain incentives under the corporate income tax within a province, we are going to benefit by trying to take away from one province for the benefit of another. Certainly, the robbing of one brother by another does not lead to any advantage.
I thank you for your indulgence, Mr. Chairman, in allowing me this digression. I wanted to put this on the record because it has been

a very distressing development in our interprovincial and federal relationships over the past three years. If there are any changes to be made in the constitution, if there is a price to be paid for this repatriation, then I would suggest that one of the changes that might be made would be the reaffirmation of this freedom of interprovincial trade. There should not be tolerated any direct or indirect barriers to trade flowing within the country and we should do away with these narrow, regional interests which, frankly, lead only to divide our national purpose.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to make a speech. I should simply like to put a question to the Minister of Justice. I would like to ask him whether it is the government's policy or whether he believes it would be easier to find an amending formula for the constitution after its repatriation, or if it would be just as easy to find such a formula after it is repatriated? Would it not be the first thing to do? First, repatriate the constitution and then try to find an amending formula?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if you wish to have my personal opinion-and I know that some disagree-I think that in order to protect the guarantees throughout Canada, some provinces do not have the same protection nor the same guarantees which certain provinces demand. In my opinion, it would be advisable to devise a formula to amend and
Business of the House repatriate the constitution adopting such a formula at the same time.
I think that we must first of all find an amending formula, proceed to the repatriation of the constitution, and include the amending formula therein.

Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to ask the house leader the business for Thursday and Friday.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the business of the house for Thursday and Friday will be substantially what has been announced. There will be a slight modification which I am about to announce. We will begin with the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. We would then take the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, then those of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, followed by those of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
If there is some possibility of making an arrangement through the house leaders we may begin tomorrow with the motion to refer the question of the water levels to the committee on forests and waters so that this committee may begin its work as early as possible. I repeat, this will depend on whether an arrangement can be made.
